items.summary: Open the safe on the top floor of this ruined motel.

content.v: You'll need the GTA 6 La Cascara safe code if you decide to rob this tempting-looking ruined motel in Port Gellhorn. This is probably the most lucrative robbery in the town with an LMG, grenade launcher, and a unique weapon, plus a unique vehicle and a whole lot of drugs.

Thankfully, though, the safe code, which is 6969 (nice) is fixed for this robbery. As with the Brooks Boatworks safe code and the Bowling Alley safe code , you can actually find all three of these on a board in the Brooks Boatworks robbery in northwest Port Gellhorn. To find it:

Make sure to bring Jason to La Cascara when you can, since there's more than two stash bags worth of loot. Also, while you're on the top floor of La Cascara, head into the room next to the safe to find the Scrapped VF5C on the table—this silenced SMG is perhaps the best early gun I've found, simply because you can sneakily take out enemies. There's also a grenade launcher on the lower floor.

As well as those, make sure to scour the top floor, the floor below it, and the first floor, for weed, pills, sticky bombs, and lots of cash. Finally, steal the Vapid Firebug Dominator (the red and black muscle car) out front to clear all the key valuables.

items.title: 如何在 GTA 6 中找到艾利当铺安全代码
items.summary: Crack the case in the Hit Avery Pawn mission.

content.v: Chapter 2 of GTA 6 finally gives you full control over both Jason and Lucia, and one of the first missions you'll undertake as a criminal couple involves committing a robbery in one of three locations.

One of your options is Avery Pawn Shop, where you'll be able to make a tidy sum of money if you can smash-and-grab enough loot and, more crucially, find the safe code to crack it open for additional cash and jewellery.The easiest way to do that is to grab the code for the safe, which is thankfully pretty easy to do.
How to find the Avery Pawn Shop safe code
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/7YrZz3pEuAAU8AtDMkeDJY-1920-80.png
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/qvQTXPMuxHfGpMgUX4DXAY-1920-80.png
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/7FjUWMLdM5CqghtRU7tAJY-1920-80.png

Head inside Avery Pawn with your partner in tow—don't forget to pop on a mask , along with a hat and sunglasses to hide your identity—and begin holding up the store by pulling out your gun with L2 and pointing it at the clerks.

You should be able to threaten one of the staff members with Square and, with the other, the same input should instead change to "Safe Code?" if you look at the bottom-right corner. For me, it was the one standing behind the counter on the left.

The clerk should give up the safe code with little resistance. Once you have it, head behind the counter and into the back room. There'll be another staff member there, but you can point your gun and threaten him as well. Head into the office to the right, input the safe code, and grab your goods.

It looks like, at least where pawn shops are concerned, the code given is random. In my case, the code was 5683, but yours will most likely be different. This method should work for every pawn shop though, not just Avery Pawn!

items.title: GTA 6 中最不可饶恕的罪行是电视植入
items.summary: Jason and Cal do their best to redecorate the bach' pad but c'mon boys, a TV in front of a giant glass door? W

content.v: Grand Theft Auto 6 is a game about criminals doing crimes. Car crimes, gun crimes, drug crimes, and first degree decorating crimes. Early in the game, Jason's buddy Cal convinces him that he's got to turn his r/malelivingspace shack into a place he can bring his girl Lucia without feeling like she's still stuck in a jail cell. Cal is right, but his decorating decisions should be illegal.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/gzE7aecf5nV2nHJWnbqkE3-1920-80.jpg

This is how Jason's living room looks at the beginning of the game while he's still flying solo. Not great, Jason. If I've learned anything from lurking in interior decorating communities online it's that furniture should never be touching your walls, no matter how small the room is, and that nobody's TV is ever at the right height.

Cal hassles Jason into moving some things around and, while I love his motivation, he makes everything worse. What they wind up with is this: couch blocking prime navigation space and the TV sitting in front of the sliding glass door. Look, I know the point is that Cal is an incompetent dork. He's slugging beers and insisting they make the room feng shui. I can't forgive him for this one though.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/wkzxjwEVk58pEhkE4Gj7i5-1920-80.png

Cal does get one thing right here: using the couch and arm chair to create a space that feels like a living room within the open area. Once Lucia moves in she and Jason continue making the waterfront shack more homey. They get a rug in the living room, a classic choice to finish tying that space into a room. Lucia brings home a coffee table to assemble (cute domestic conversation ensues). The dining table gets centered properly in its corner.

But that damn TV stays parked in front of the glass door. It's criminal! There would be so much glare on that screen from the east and west facing windows and light all day long drowning it out from behind that north facing glass door. My sad, myopic eyes are tearing up just thinking about squinting at it.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/yxKJDH7N43yUKFB9Got66C-1920-80.png

So I took Jason's conundrum to one of the interior decorating communities on Reddit to ask for some group workshopping. They immediately grasped the unforgivable TV placement and the inherent issue with the number of windows in this place. Almost no wall is safe here.

One suggestion was to keep those window blinds in the living room down and place the TV stand in front of it. Makes sense to me—Jason wouldn't be losing much light with all the other windows in here. Another more minor fix was to just put the TV at a 45 degree angle in its corner so it's less directly in front of the glass door, though I don't think that solves the glare problems.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/RtZM2xtic2sHFmNFkjwYL5-1920-80.png

The more popular suggestion (and my favorite) was to swap the dining and living room. The TV can sit on the rear wall, slightly tucked away with the blinds pulled down, while the dining table gets easier access from the kitchen and doesn't suffer for being lit from all sides.

Alas, I have it on good authority that the TV never manages to move from where Cal stuck it. I can forgive drug smuggling, but I draw the line at suboptimal viewing angles. Ah well, perhaps Jason and Lucia have a better floor plan to work with in the next place they move to as their criminal exploits grow.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/BHPqKqLPfA5ZBPetGie6Zb-1920-80.jpg

items.title: 当我还是个孩子的时候，我的阁楼里没有怪物，我有一个局域网
items.summary: I'm not boasting. OK, I am a bit.

content.v: Weird Weekend is our regular Saturday column where we celebrate PC gaming oddities: peculiar games, strange bits of trivia, forgotten history. Pop back every weekend to find out what Jeremy, Josh, Rick and Ted have become obsessed with this time, whether it's the canon height of Thief's Garrett or that time someone in the Vatican pirated Football Manager .

Multiplayer gaming on PC these days is so easy you probably barely even think about it. Most games that support multiplayer will work out of the gate, and there's an abundance of ways to connect and chat with your friends across the globe. This is a far cry from the early days of PC multiplayer, when dial-up connections and ad-hoc servers made multiplayer PC gaming expensive and unreliable.

Indeed, the best way to play multiplayer PC games back then was via a LAN. A local network offered the fastest and most stable connections, and didn't cost you anything beyond the hardware required to hook it all together. Unfortunately, it was also the least convenient way of playing PC games with your friends, as it meant one or several of you had to haul your whole-ass PC to an agreed-upon location.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/bbcM2WRFpDZoBw2LKtfzM9-1920-80.jpg

Because of this, LAN gaming was a rare treat for most people in the '90s and early '00s. Unless, that is, you happened to be a disgustingly lucky bastard like myself, and had a LAN in your attic that you could play at any time.

Now, this sounds like the kind of lie a 10-year-old would blurt out in the playground to impress his friends (specifically, an eight-year-old from the mid '90s who had a working knowledge of PC gaming, which, I concede, is a limited demographic) and indeed, the further away I get from that time, the more like a false memory it seems. But it is 100% true, and I have the pictures to prove it.

The LAN (as it was simply and practically known) was in service between 2001 and 2003, and existed because of my family's long-running enthusiasm for PCs and PC gaming. As I've mentioned in other articles, my dad was fascinated by the internet from 1994 onward, both just as a technology and for the business opportunities it offered. Meanwhile, his brother (my uncle) was an IT support expert and a dedicated PC gamer.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ifKH2PSFssqAvB8bWtPzo8-1920-80.jpg

Since they were close as siblings and shared this mutual interest (at least on the PC aspect—my dad was never much of a gamer) there was a constant stream of PC hardware flowing through the house, as they tried to keep up with the rapid progress of PCs through the '90s. Eventually, when they'd upgrade a PC, they began taking the old components and building them into a "new" PCs. This is how my brother and I ended with our joint PC in 1997, and how we ended up with individual PCs a few years later.

In 2000 my family (and, separately, my uncle) moved to the Isle of Man, which for non UK audiences is a small island between Britain and Ireland known for two things: tail-less cats and incredibly dangerous motorbike races. The house we rented there had a converted attic—complete with creaky, bare-floorboard stairs—and my dad decided this was the ideal space to set up all three PCs.

Initially the PCs weren't connected. But the layout of the room meant it was only a matter of time before my dad and uncle had that particular brainwave. At some point in 2001, another upgrade happened, and we were left with spare parts for a fourth PC, which could be used as a dedicated server to network the other three PCs together.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/TaaKeAqk63bpsjniJrGJM9-1920-80.jpg

The upshot was we had a three-PC LAN on which we could play multiplayer games. I have a distinct memory of them clunking about in the attic while setting this up—likely over a weekend or possibly that year's Easter holiday. I also remember them showing it to us once they were done and explaining how it all worked.

What I don't remember, annoyingly, is what the first game we played on it was. It might have been Doom, though I can't say for certain. I think the reason I don't remember is that once the LAN was set up, my brother and I were largely left to our own devices to get games running on it. Hence, a lot of my memories surrounding the LAN are about that , rather than the games we actually played.

Even with the hard work of setting up the LAN done, getting games to work on it often proved a challenge. Since each PC was the product of multiple rounds of leftovers, they all had different components, so the chance of encountering compatibility issues with a game on at least one of the PCs was not insignificant. The difference between a 1998 PC and a 2001 PC was cavernous, so they might have a processor that was too old, a graphics card that didn't support the latest DirectX, insufficient RAM.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/kxJK6RFASfAMXQewNLkRy8-1920-80.jpg

In addition, while we had three PCs, we'd typically only have one copy of any given game, which meant rolling the dice on copy protection with every game we tried (and occasionally searching the murkier corners of the Internet for a crack or a keygen— don't tell the police .) Even if the game installed successfully, there would often be a question of whether it could find the dedicated server on each PC, or whether I'd have to go futzing around in the network settings—not an easy thing to do when you're 13 and stupid.

Nonetheless, there were quite a few games that made it all the way through the gauntlet. The one I remember most vividly is Half-Life: Opposing Force deathmatch—which was basically Half-Life deathmatch with more maps and more weapons. One of OpFor's multiplayer maps, Datacore , was the perfect size for three players, and we'd spend hours setting up laser traps for one another around the map's tight, electric-blue corridors. Another favourite was Paradox Park , which we spent ages in despite the fact it was impractically large for three players.

Pragmatism influenced what we played a lot. While my brother and I never struggled to fill that third chair (weirdly, it isn't hard to get other kids to come around to your house when you have a LAN in your attic), three players was a challenging number with a lot of games, so we tended to play stuff that had a small-scale deathmatch. That said, we definitely attempted some lopsided rounds of Counter-Strike , each taking it in turns to be the odd one out. Any game with bots, like Unreal Tournament , we considered sacred.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/6BEY7RjbgyfvfWB6b3Kri8-1920-80.jpg

Some of the stuff we played was just weird . There was a Half-Life mod called Firearms , which just had a shitload of guns in it, that we sank hours into. At one point I got super into Operation Flashpoint's map editor, and—influenced by watching Enemy at the Gates—created multiplayer sniper duels where two or three players would play lethal hide and seek in one of its various low-poly towns. When there wasn't a third player available, my brother and I would spend hours hacking each other to bits in Severance: Blade of Darkness' multiplayer duel mode. Did you know that Severance: Blade of Darkness had a multiplayer duel mode? We certainly did, and I think we probably played it more than anybody else.

Looking back, it's wild how hacky the whole experience was. Not the LAN itself—that always worked fine. But how our requirements versus the limitations of what was available affected what we played. Our siloed, odd-numbered setup was perfectly suited for the kind of modern, cooperative gaming experience that did not exist at all back then. But in some ways that was part of the magic. Any new game we got, we'd check the back of the box to see if it had a multiplayer mode and how many players it supported. If we could install and run it on all three PCs and see the host server, holy shit, that was almost as thrilling as playing the game itself.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/2F3DPxcQUbcGHs6ZrPSHp8-1920-80.jpg
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/6offQUY4CXebir2TC27dMd-1920-80.jpg

content.v: SWiitching it up.

Many people reading this will have a Wii in the house. Even if it's collecting dust in the cupboard after launching 20 years ago, there's over 100 million of the things out in the wild, so the chances are that you or your family have access to one somewhere.

However, on the off-chance you don't have a Wii to hand — or you sold it years ago to save three DVDs' worth of space — don't fret. While the system has a selection of exclusives you can't easily play elsewhere, many Wii games have come to Switch in HD remastered form over the years.
